cards.prompt: A chatbot can write a great answer with one wrong number hidden in it. One says: "3 boxes of 24 pencils is **62** pencils." Check its maths. How many pencils is it really?
cards.hint: Work it out yourself: 3 lots of 24.
cards.explanation: 3 × 24 = **72**, not 62. A chatbot predicts likely-looking words, and a likely-looking number isn't always the right one. So do the maths yourself.

cards.title: Four ways to check
cards.body:
Chatbots can sound sure and be wrong. Check:

- **Facts and dates:** find them in a trusted source, like a textbook or official website.
- **Sources:** open each one and read it.
- **Maths:** work it out yourself.
- **News and "latest":** a model learned from text up to a certain date. Unless it searches the web, it may not know what's happened since.

cards.prompt: The chatbot's paragraph says: "The Moon is about 38,000 km from Earth, and it takes about 3 days to get there by spacecraft."

steps.text: It sounds fine. What do you do with that distance?

choices.text: Keep it: a second chatbot gave the same distance
choices.consequence: Two chatbots can make the same mistake, so agreeing isn't checking. A trusted source says about 384,000 km, ten times further.

choices.text: Look it up on a space agency website
choices.consequence: It says the Moon is about **384,000 km** away on average. The chatbot dropped a digit.

choices.text: Ask it to show how it worked out the distance
choices.consequence: It writes neat, confident working that ends at 38,000 km again. Its working is more predicted words, so it can't check its own number.

cards.hint: Which of the four checks fits a fact like a distance?
cards.explanation: The Moon is about **384,000 km** away on average, not 38,000. Numbers are easy to get wrong and hard to spot, so check them in a **trusted source**, like a space agency's website. A second chatbot, or the chatbot's own working, isn't a check.

cards.prompt: A chatbot tells you the newest model of a phone "came out last month". What's the **main** reason to check that?

options.text: It may have mixed up this phone with an older model with a similar name
options.nudge: That can happen, but it isn't the main risk with "last month". When did the model learn?

options.text: It learned from text up to a certain date, so "last month" may be long gone
It can't tell what today's date is, so it makes up every date at random
options.nudge: Its dates aren't random: they come from the text it learned from. When did it learn?

options.text: A high temperature may have made it pick an unlikely release date
options.nudge: Temperature changes how it picks, but even at low temperature what might it be missing?

cards.hint: Look back at the four checks. Which one is about news and "latest" things?
cards.explanation: A model learned from text up to a certain date. Unless it can search the web, "the newest" and "last month" mean newest **when it learned**, which may be long before today.

cards.prompt: Using AI to **learn** is great: it can explain a step, quiz you, or give feedback on your draft. Letting it **do your work**, and handing that in as yours, is different, and many schools have rules about AI. Which is each one?

items.label: Asking it to explain a maths step
Getting it to quiz you on your notes
Asking for feedback on your draft
Handing in its essay as yours
Getting it to answer a take-home test
Rewording its essay to sound like you

cards.hint: Who ends up doing the thinking in each one: you, or the chatbot?
cards.nudge: Look at who ends up doing the thinking and the writing in each one.
cards.explanation: Explanations, quizzes and feedback help **you** think. Handing in its essay, letting it do a test, or rewording its essay to sound like you all let it **do the work**, however it's dressed up.

cards.prompt: Match each thing a chatbot told you to the **best** way to check it.

pairs.right: Look it up in a textbook or museum site

pairs.left: A link it gave as its source
pairs.right: Open it and read what it says

cards.hint: Use the four checks. Which one fits each kind of claim?
cards.nudge: A link is a source to read, a sum you can do yourself, and recent news needs something dated.
cards.explanation: Dates go to a **trusted source** like a textbook or museum site; sums you **work out yourself**; links you **open and read**; and recent news needs a **dated** source, because the chatbot may have learned before it happened.

cards.prompt: Your friend shows you an essay a chatbot wrote for them, due tomorrow.

steps.text: "I'm handing this in as mine. It's fine, everyone does it." What do you say?

choices.text: "OK, but at least read it through before you hand it in"
choices.consequence: Reading it is a start, but it's still the chatbot's work handed in as theirs. That may break the school's rules, and they miss the learning.

choices.text: "Check the AI rules. Use it to plan, then write your own"
choices.consequence: Good: you didn't lecture, you gave them an honest way to use it.

choices.text: "Add a few sentences of your own so it's partly yours"
choices.consequence: Most of it is still the chatbot's work, handed in as theirs. A few extra sentences don't change that.

cards.hint: Think about honest ways to use AI, and the school's rules.
cards.explanation: Handing in AI's work as your own can break school rules, and you miss the learning. An honest option: **check the rules**, use AI to plan or explain, and write it yourself.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Check facts in a trusted source, and do the maths yourself.
- A model learned up to a certain date: be careful with "latest".
- Use AI to learn, not to do your work.

Next: the AI tools around today.
